facts.text: In a time bank, members earn one time credit for every hour spent helping another member, and spend credits on help from anyone else in the group; no money changes hands.
Time banking follows the principle of equal time, equal value: an hour of a computer specialist’s work counts the same as an hour of cleaning.
American law professor Edgar Cahn coined the term time banking in 1980; he set it up to build community and meet social needs at a time when social services were being cut.
Similar exchanges of labor for labor had roots in 19th-century labor reform movements in America and Europe, in the 1800s.
With Spanish unemployment near 25 percent around 2012, the number of time banks in Spain doubled in two years to nearly 300; most had between 50 and 400 members.

A mother in Madrid whose teenage son uses a wheelchair lost a daily nurse when public spending was cut; time bank members helped lift her son, and she repaid them by driving disabled people in her specially fitted car.
In Spain, time bank services had to stay occasional so that they did not compete unfairly with businesses that pay tax.
The Charlotte County Time Bank in New Brunswick, Canada, was founded after its founder broke both wrists and needed help with everyday tasks at home.
Members of the Charlotte County Time Bank have exchanged rides to medical appointments, baking, gardening, snow clearing and skateboarding lessons.
A board member of the Charlotte County Time Bank says that requesting help also helps others, because it lets them earn hours.
A study of six timebanks in England found that many members only wanted to offer help and did not request services, which slowed timebank activity.
A sociologist says most time banks do not last long, and the most successful ones have official hosts and infrastructure.
Reviews of time banks report problems such as members hoarding credits and few places to spend them.
